definitions.explanation: A traditional Japanese pipe with a small metal bowl and long bamboo stem, used for smoking finely shredded tobacco.

Slang for riding a train while only paying for the first and last portions of the journey, skipping the fare for the middle section. Named because a kiseru pipe has metal at both ends and bamboo in the middle — like a ticket that only covers the endpoints.

examples.japanese: {煙管|きせる}で{煙草|たばこ}を{吸|す}う。
examples.english: To smoke tobacco with a kiseru pipe.

examples.japanese: {江戸|えど}{時代|じだい}の{人々|ひとびと}は{煙管|きせる}を{日常的|にちじょうてき}に{使|つか}っていた。
examples.english: People in the Edo period used kiseru pipes daily.

examples.japanese: {骨董品|こっとうひん}{店|てん}で{美|うつく}しい{蒔絵|まきえ}の{煙管|きせる}を{見|み}つけた。
examples.english: I found a beautiful maki-e lacquered kiseru at an antique shop.

examples.japanese: {煙管|きせる}{乗車|じょうしゃ}は{犯罪|はんざい}だ。
{煙管|きせる}をして{捕|つか}まった。
examples.english: He got caught evading the fare.

examples.japanese: ICカードの{普及|ふきゅう}で{煙管|きせる}{乗車|じょうしゃ}は{難|むずか}しくなった。
examples.english: The spread of IC cards has made fare evasion more difficult.

notes: The word comes from Cambodian (khsier). The kanji {煙管|きせる} is an ateji reading. For the fare evasion sense, the metaphor is: a kiseru has metal ({金|かね}) at both ends with bamboo ({竹|たけ}) in the middle — like paying ({金|かね} also means 'money') only for the start and end stations. Common collocations: {煙管|きせる}{乗車|じょうしゃ} (fare evasion by train), {煙管|きせる}をする (to evade the fare).
